title: Data Storytelling and Dashboard Design
subtitle: Turn analysis into a clear message for a real audience: choose and declutter charts, build a narrative that leads to a decision, and design honest, accessible KPI dashboards.
outcomes: Turn a vague request into a question tied to a decision, and state the answer as one big idea for a named audience
Choose charts by the comparison they must show, then declutter them, use colour for meaning and write action titles
Structure a data story as situation, complication and resolution, and present or write it so the audience can act
Choose, define and lay out KPIs on a one-page dashboard that shows the most important information first
Make charts accessible and honest, recognising and fixing truncated axes, dual axes and other misleading designs
prerequisites: No coding is needed: the labs give Python code and spreadsheet formulas (Excel, Google Sheets or LibreOffice Calc). For Python, you need basic pandas, as in Data Analysis with Python and pandas, and Python 3 with pandas and Matplotlib. For spreadsheets, SUMIFS and pivot tables, as in Spreadsheet Data Analysis: Formulas, Pivot Tables and Charts. The data comes with the labs.
description:
Analysis only helps when someone understands it and acts on it. This course is about that last step: turning numbers into a message for a particular audience, and into dashboards people can read at a glance. You'll work with two years of figures from Lantern Lane, a made-up online homeware shop whose owners asked a simple question, 'how did 2025 go?', which hides a better story: revenue grew but missed its target, the marketplace boomed, and a website redesign quietly cost hundreds of orders. You'll learn to turn a vague request into a question with a decision behind it, to know your audience, to state your answer as one big idea and to choose the chart that carries it; then to declutter it, use colour only to mean something and write titles that say what the chart shows.

Next you'll build a narrative with situation, complication and resolution, order charts so their titles alone tell the story, and write a one-page summary that leads to a decision. You'll design a KPI dashboard: what it's for, which KPIs deserve a place, how to define them precisely and how to lay them out. The last module covers accessibility (contrast, never colour alone, alternative text) and the charts that mislead without a false number, from truncated axes to dual axes and cumulative lines. Every lab works in Python or a spreadsheet and has exact figures to check, and the capstone is a dashboard, a story and a summary for the shop's owners. It suits analysts, managers and anyone who presents data; Data Visualisation with Matplotlib, Seaborn and Plotly goes deeper into building charts in code.

modules.title: From question to message
modules.summary: Turn a vague request into a question with a decision behind it, know exactly who you're telling, and boil the answer down to one sentence and the chart that carries it.

lessons.title: Exploratory and explanatory: start with the decision
objectives: Distinguish exploratory analysis from explanatory communication
Turn a vague request into a specific question tied to a decision
Agree the question, the comparison and the deadline before analysing
key_points: Exploratory analysis is how you find out what's in the data, making many charts for yourself; explanatory communication shows an audience the few findings that matter, so it uses far fewer charts, each designed to make one point.
Behind every request is a decision: 'can you look at sales?' becomes useful once you know who will decide what, such as whether to keep a website redesign or move budget to the marketplace.

A specific question names the measure, the comparison, the group and the period: 'Did website conversion fall after June's redesign, compared with January to May?' can be answered; 'How are sales?' cannot.
Agree the question, what comparison will count as an answer and the deadline with whoever asked, before analysing; it saves building charts nobody needs.
Write the question at the top of your notes and test each finding against it: interesting results that don't help the decision belong in an appendix or a later conversation.

lessons.title: Knowing your audience
objectives: Describe an audience by what they know, what they care about and what they must do
Adapt the level of detail and the medium to the audience
Avoid the curse of knowledge
key_points: Picture one specific audience: what they already know, what they care about (money, customers, risk, their team) and what you need them to do or decide afterwards.
A mixed audience splits the message: lead with what the decision-maker needs, and put the detail that specialists want in an appendix or a follow-up.

The medium changes the design: a live presentation can build a chart step by step while you talk, a document or email must explain itself without you, and a dashboard is read again and again with nobody there to explain it.
The curse of knowledge, finding it hard to imagine not knowing what you know, makes analysts skip steps and use jargon; define terms such as conversion rate in plain words the first time they appear.
Decision-makers usually want the conclusion and what it means for them first, and specialists may want the method; ask, or look at what the audience has responded to before, rather than guessing.

lessons.title: The big idea, and the chart that carries it
objectives: Write the main message as one complete sentence with a point of view and what's at stake
Choose a chart by the comparison the message makes
Show the comparison that matters directly
key_points: The big idea is one complete sentence that states your point of view and what's at stake, such as 'Revenue grew 6.5% but missed its target because a website fault cut conversion for four months, so test checkout before every release.'
If you can't say the message in a sentence, or explain it in about three minutes, the analysis isn't finished: a list of facts is not yet a message.

Choose the chart by the comparison in the message: change over time as a line, actuals against a target as bars with target marks, a ranking as sorted bars, a change between two moments as a slope chart, and one key number as the number itself, large.

Plot the comparison readers must make: if the message is how this year differs from last, draw both years on the same axes, or chart the difference itself, instead of asking readers to compare two separate charts.
A line chart's axis can start above zero to show a change clearly, because readers judge a line by its position, not its length; a bar chart's can't.

lab.title: Find the message in a year of shop data
lab.goal: Lantern Lane's owners asked 'how did 2025 go?'. Turn that into specific questions, find the facts with Python or spreadsheet formulas, write the big idea in one sentence and make the one chart that carries it.
setup: The starter files: monthly_channels.csv (visits, orders, revenue and returns by month and sales channel for a made-up online homeware shop, 2024 to 2025), targets_2025.csv (its monthly revenue targets for 2025) and findings.py
Python route: Python 3 with pandas and matplotlib in a virtual environment
Spreadsheet route: Excel, Google Sheets or LibreOffice Calc, with both CSV files imported, each on its own sheet

steps.do: Before touching the data, write down the decision behind 'how did 2025 go?' and three specific questions, each naming a measure, a comparison and a period. For example: did 2025 revenue beat 2024's and the target?
Python route: run the starter, which prints the yearly totals.
steps.code: python findings.py
steps.see: Visits, orders and revenue for 2024 and 2025: 420323 and 447471 in the revenue column.

steps.do: Add the comparison with last year and with the target.
steps.code:
# 1. How did 2025 compare with 2024, and with the target?
revenue = ch.groupby("year")["revenue"].sum()
target = targets["revenue_target"].sum()
print(f"Revenue 2025: £{revenue[2025]:,.0f}, {revenue[2025] / revenue[2024] - 1:+.1%} on 2024")
print(f"Target 2025: £{target:,.0f}; revenue was £{target - revenue[2025]:,.0f} short ({revenue[2025] / target:.1%} of target)")

steps.do: Add the change by channel, sorted from the biggest rise.
steps.code:
# 2. Which channels drove the change?
by_channel = ch.pivot_table(index="channel", columns="year", values="revenue", aggfunc="sum")
by_channel["change"] = by_channel[2025] / by_channel[2024] - 1
for channel, row in by_channel.sort_values("change", ascending=False).iterrows():
    print(f"{channel:12} £{row[2024]:>9,.0f} -> £{row[2025]:>9,.0f}  {row['change']:+.1%}")
steps.see: marketplace +34.8%, social +11.0% and website -6.2%

steps.do: The website fell although its visits rose, so add its conversion rate (orders ÷ visits) for 2024 and three periods of 2025.
steps.code:
# 3. Why did the website fall? Its conversion rate (orders / visits), period by period
web = ch[ch["channel"] == "website"].copy()
web["period"] = "2024"
web.loc[(web["year"] == 2025) & (web["month"] <= 5), "period"] = "2025 Jan-May"
web.loc[(web["year"] == 2025) & web["month"].between(6, 9), "period"] = "2025 Jun-Sep"
web.loc[(web["year"] == 2025) & (web["month"] >= 10), "period"] = "2025 Oct-Dec"
conv = web.groupby("period")[["orders", "visits"]].sum()
conv["conversion"] = conv["orders"] / conv["visits"]
print(conv["conversion"].map("{:.2%}".format).to_string())

steps.do: Spreadsheet route: work out the same figures with SUMIFS. In a spreadsheet, the columns of monthly_channels.csv are A year, B month, C channel, D visits, E orders, F revenue and G returns. In LibreOffice Calc, use semicolons between the arguments if your settings ask for them.

2025 revenue:        =SUMIFS(F:F, A:A, 2025)
Change on 2024:      =SUMIFS(F:F, A:A, 2025) / SUMIFS(F:F, A:A, 2024) - 1
Marketplace change:  =SUMIFS(F:F, A:A, 2025, C:C, "marketplace") / SUMIFS(F:F, A:A, 2024, C:C, "marketplace") - 1
Website conversion, June to September 2025:

   / SUMIFS(D:D, A:A, 2025, C:C, "website", B:B, ">=6", B:B, "<=9")
2025 target (on the targets sheet, revenue_target in column C):  =SUM(C:C)
steps.see: 447,471.27; 6.5%; 34.8%; 2.12%; 470,900, once formatted as numbers and percentages.

steps.do: Write the big idea in one sentence: your point of view, the key numbers and what's at stake. Keep it in big_idea.txt.

Python route: make the one chart that carries the message: this year's website conversion against last year's, with the redesign period shaded and the finding as the title. Spreadsheet route: make the same line chart from a small table of monthly conversion rates.
steps.code:
# 4. One chart that carries the message: this year's conversion against last year's
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

web["conversion"] = web["orders"] / web["visits"] * 100
before, during = conv.loc["2025 Jan-May", "conversion"], conv.loc["2025 Jun-Sep", "conversion"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4), layout="constrained")
for year, colour in [(2024, "#BBBBBB"), (2025, "#0072B2")]:
    d = web[web["year"] == year]
    ax.plot(d["month"], d["conversion"], color=colour, linewidth=2.5 if year == 2025 else 1.5, marker="o")
    ax.text(12.3, d["conversion"].iloc[-1], str(year), va="center", fontweight="bold",
            color="#0072B2" if year == 2025 else "#595959")
ax.axvspan(5.5, 9.5, color="#E69F00", alpha=0.15, linewidth=0)
ax.text(5.7, 3.15, "New website design in June;\ncheckout fixed in October", fontsize=9, color="#595959", va="top")
ax.set_xticks(range(1, 13), ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun", "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"])
ax.set_ylim(1.5, 3.2)
ax.set_ylabel("Website conversion rate (%)")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.set_title(f"Website conversion fell from {before:.1%} to {during:.1%} after the June redesign", loc="left")
fig.savefig("message_chart.png", dpi=150)
print("Saved message_chart.png:", ax.get_title(loc="left"))
steps.see: Saved message_chart.png: Website conversion fell from 2.8% to 2.1% after the June redesign

checks.text: 2025 revenue and its change on 2024 are right.
The comparison with the target is right: a target of 470,900, missed by about 23,429.
The channel changes show the marketplace growing and the website falling.
Website conversion is worked out for each period.
The chart's title states the finding.

hints: A big idea has a verb and a point of view: 'Website conversion' is a topic; 'Website conversion fell after the redesign and cost us the target' is a message.
Percentages of totals can't be averaged across months: work out conversion as total orders ÷ total visits for the period, as the script and the SUMIFS formulas do.
If a spreadsheet shows 0.0212 instead of 2.12%, format the cell as a percentage with two decimal places.
If SUMIFS returns 0, check that year and month were imported as numbers, not text (numbers align right by default).

modules.title: Decluttering, colour and annotation
modules.summary: Strip a chart back to what helps the reader, use colour only where it means something, and write titles and labels that say what the chart shows.

lessons.title: Decluttering: less ink, less effort
objectives: Explain how clutter adds to the reader's effort
Remove borders, heavy gridlines, markers and legends that don't help
Use the Gestalt principles of proximity, similarity, enclosure and connection to group information
key_points: Every element on a chart costs the reader attention, so anything that doesn't help them understand the data, such as borders, heavy gridlines, background shading, markers on every point or 3-D effects, is clutter to remove.

Edward Tufte's idea of data-ink is a useful test: how much of the ink on the chart shows data? Raise the share by removing or lightening the rest, while keeping what readers need, such as an axis to read values from.
Label lines directly at their ends instead of using a legend, and remove axis titles that repeat what's obvious, such as 'Month' under twelve month names.

Gestalt principles describe how people group what they see: things close together (proximity), alike in colour or shape (similarity), inside one box (enclosure) or joined by a line (connection) are read as belonging together.
Align titles, labels and charts to a common left edge and leave white space around them: alignment and space create order without adding any ink.

walkthrough.title: Declutter a line chart in Google Sheets

steps.do: Open a new spreadsheet (sheets.new), choose File > Import > Upload and upload monthly_channels.csv from the module 1 lab files; choose Replace spreadsheet and Import data.

Select the data and choose Insert > Pivot table > Create. In the pivot table editor, add year and month under Rows, channel under Columns and revenue under Values (summarised by SUM), and untick Show totals for both rows and columns.
steps.see: A table with one row per month and a column per channel.

steps.do: Click inside the pivot table and choose Insert > Chart. In the chart editor's Setup tab, choose Line chart.
steps.see: A line per channel, with a legend and the default colours.

steps.do: In the Customise tab, open Series and pick each channel in turn: a light grey for website and social, and a strong blue with a thicker line for marketplace, the series the message is about.
Open Gridlines and ticks: for the vertical axis, set the major gridline colour to a light grey; for the horizontal axis, untick the major gridlines.
Open Chart & axis titles. Choose Chart title and type the finding, Marketplace sales grew 35% in 2025; then choose Chart subtitle and type Monthly revenue by sales channel, £.
Open Legend and set its position to Top, so it's read before the lines, or to None if the title already names the highlighted series.
Open Vertical axis and check that the minimum is 0 or blank, then compare the result with the default chart: same data, far less to decode.

lessons.title: Colour with meaning
objectives: Use colour to highlight, not to decorate
Keep colours consistent across a set of charts
Choose colours whose meaning readers will share
key_points: Start every chart in grey and add colour only where you want the eye to go: one accent colour for the series or bar that carries the message, with everything else as context.
Use the same colour for the same thing in every chart of a report or dashboard, such as blue always meaning the marketplace, so readers don't have to relearn the colours on each page.

Colours carry associations that differ between readers and cultures, such as red for danger or loss in many places but for good fortune in others, so don't rely on them alone: say 'good' or 'bad' in words, or with arrows, too.
Use colour intensity for order: a sequential palette (light to dark) for low-to-high values, and a diverging palette, with a neutral midpoint, for values above and below a target or zero.
Brand colours are a starting point, not a rule: if a brand palette is too pale against white or hard to tell apart, use darker shades of it for data and keep the light ones for backgrounds.

lessons.title: Titles, labels and annotation
objectives: Write action titles that state the finding
Format numbers, units and dates so they're read at a glance
Annotate the one point that matters most
key_points: An action title states the finding, as in 'Marketplace sales grew 35% in 2025, while website sales fell 6%'; a subtitle then gives the measure, units and period, and a footnote the source.
Round numbers to what the decision needs (£447k, not £447,471.27), give units and currency once, use thousands separators and write dates the same way throughout.

Annotate the point the message depends on, such as the month of a website redesign, with a short note beside the data rather than in a separate key: a shaded band marks a period and a reference line a target.
Write labels in plain language, such as 'conversion rate (orders as a share of visits)', not field names from a database such as conv_rt.
Many readers read only the title, so check that each chart's title would make sense, and still be true, if it were the only thing they saw.

files.content:
"""Make over a cluttered chart of Lantern Lane's revenue by channel."""
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
from matplotlib.colors import to_hex


def audit(fig, name):
    """Print what a chart contains, to compare the cluttered version with the clean one."""
    for ax in fig.axes:
        spines = [side for side, spine in ax.spines.items() if spine.get_visible()]
        colours = {to_hex(line.get_color()) for line in ax.get_lines()}
        colours |= {to_hex(bar.get_facecolor()) for bar in ax.patches}
        xgrid = any(g.get_visible() for g in ax.xaxis.get_gridlines())
        ygrid = any(g.get_visible() for g in ax.yaxis.get_gridlines())
        grid = "x and y" if xgrid and ygrid else "y only" if ygrid else "x only" if xgrid else "none"
        print(f"{name}: title {ax.get_title(loc='left') or ax.get_title()!r}")
        print(f"  spines: {', '.join(spines) or 'none'}; legend: {'yes' if ax.get_legend() is not None else 'none'}; "
              f"gridlines: {grid}; colours: {len(colours)}; text labels: {len(ax.texts)}")


ch = pd.read_csv("monthly_channels.csv")
ch["date"] = pd.to_datetime(dict(year=ch["year"], month=ch["month"], day=1))
wide = ch.pivot_table(index="date", columns="channel", values="revenue", aggfunc="sum")

# The "before" chart: every default left on, plus some extra clutter
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
wide.plot(ax=ax, marker="o")
ax.grid(True)
ax.set_title("Revenue by Channel")
ax.set_ylabel("revenue")
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelrotation=45)
fig.savefig("before.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
audit(fig, "before")
plt.close(fig)

hints: If the labels at the ends of the lines overlap, nudge one up or down by adding or subtracting a little from its y value.
ax.set_title(..., pad=24) leaves room above the plot for the subtitle that ax.text places at y=1.03.
Highlighting is a choice about the message: to tell the website's story instead, make the website line the accent and the marketplace grey.

modules.title: Building the narrative
modules.summary: Give a data story a beginning, a middle and an end, order the charts so their titles alone tell the story, and present or write it up so the audience can act.

lessons.title: Story structure: setup, conflict and resolution
objectives: Structure a data story with a beginning, a middle and an end
Use situation, complication and resolution to frame a recommendation
Choose between giving the answer first and building up to it
key_points: A story has a beginning that sets the scene, a middle with tension (something has changed or gone wrong) and an end that resolves it; in a data story, the resolution is what the audience should do.

Situation, complication, resolution (SCR) is a compact version: the situation everyone agrees on (sales grew), the complication that raises the question (but missed the target, because conversion fell) and the resolution that answers it (fix checkout and test it before every release).
Barbara Minto's pyramid principle puts the answer first, then the grouped reasons that support it, which suits busy decision-makers who may stop reading after the first paragraph.
Building up to the answer step by step suits audiences who need persuading, or who would reject a surprising conclusion heard first; the order of the evidence then does the persuading.
Tension drives attention: say clearly what is at stake, such as the revenue lost or the target missed, because a story without a problem gives the audience no reason to act.

lessons.title: Sequencing charts into a storyline
objectives: Storyboard a story before making any slides or charts
Write titles so that reading them in order tells the story
Use progressive reveal to walk an audience through a chart
key_points: Storyboard first, on paper or sticky notes: one box per point, in order, each with its title and a sketch of its chart; reordering notes is far quicker than reordering finished slides.
One chart, one point: if a chart is trying to make two points, split it; if two charts make the same point, keep the clearer one.
Write the titles so that reading only the titles, in order, tells the whole story (sometimes called horizontal logic); then check that each chart's content proves its own title (vertical logic).
Progressive reveal builds a chart in steps while you talk, such as last year's line first, then this year's, then the shaded redesign period, so the audience looks where you're talking.

Keep the design consistent from chart to chart: the same colours for the same things, the same scales where charts are compared and titles in the same place, so the audience follows the story, not the formatting.

lessons.title: Presenting and writing it up
objectives: Write a one-page summary that leads with the recommendation
Present a chart by talking the audience through it
State uncertainty and limitations honestly
key_points: A one-page summary leads with the recommendation and the big idea, gives the two or three supporting findings with their key numbers, and ends with the decision needed, who owns it and by when.
When presenting a chart, first say what it shows (the axes, and what a line or bar stands for), then point out the finding, then say what it means for the audience; never read out every number.
State uncertainty plainly: an estimate such as 'about 510 lost orders' assumes conversion would have stayed at its January to May level, and the summary should say so.

Separate what the data shows from what you infer: the data shows conversion fell after the redesign; that the redesign caused it is a conclusion supported by the timing and the recovery after the fix, not proven by the chart alone.
Put detail in an appendix, such as methods, definitions and extra breakdowns, so the main story stays short while sceptical readers can still check the work.

lab.title: Build a three-chart story
lab.goal: Storyboard and build a three-chart story for Lantern Lane's owners, in situation, complication and resolution order, estimate what the website fault cost, and check that the titles alone tell the story.
setup: The starter files: story.py, monthly_channels.csv and targets_2025.csv
Python route: Python 3 with pandas and matplotlib
Spreadsheet route: the two CSV files imported into Excel, Google Sheets or LibreOffice Calc

steps.do: Storyboard on paper first: three boxes for situation, complication and resolution, each with a draft title and a sketch of its chart.
Python route: run the starter, which loads the data and defines finish(), the shared design every chart uses.
steps.code: python story.py
steps.see: No output yet.

steps.do: Chart 1, the situation: monthly revenue in 2025 against the target, as grey bars with dark target marks.
steps.code:
# Chart 1, the context: monthly revenue against the target
monthly = y2025.groupby("month")["revenue"].sum()
target = targets.set_index("month")["revenue_target"]
growth = monthly.sum() / ch.loc[ch["year"] == 2024, "revenue"].sum() - 1

modules.title: Dashboards and KPIs
modules.summary: Decide what a dashboard is for, choose and define the few KPIs that matter, and lay them out so the most important information is seen first.

lessons.title: What a dashboard is for
objectives: Distinguish operational, strategic and analytical dashboards
Define a dashboard's users, decisions and refresh rate before designing it
Explain how a dashboard differs from a report or a presentation
key_points: A dashboard shows the most important information someone needs to monitor, arranged on one screen so it can be taken in at a glance (a definition popularised by Stephen Few); unlike a presentation, it's read again and again, with nobody there to explain it.

Operational dashboards track what's happening now, such as today's orders or stock, and are checked often; strategic dashboards track progress towards goals, usually monthly; analytical dashboards let analysts filter and explore.
Start with the users and their decisions: who opens it, how often and what they'll do differently depending on what they see; a measure nobody acts on doesn't belong on it.
Match the data's refresh rate to the decisions: a monthly review needs monthly figures, and hourly data on it only adds noise; show on the dashboard when the data was last updated.
A dashboard answers 'how are we doing?' but rarely 'why?', so pair it with analysis or a story when something changes, and link to the detail.

lessons.title: Choosing and defining KPIs
objectives: Choose KPIs that are tied to goals and can be acted on
Write precise KPI definitions
Give every KPI a comparison: a target, the previous period or the same period last year
key_points: A key performance indicator (KPI) is a measure tied to a goal that someone can act on, such as website conversion rate for a sales goal; a vanity metric, such as total page views, can rise while the business gets worse.

Define each KPI precisely and once: the formula (orders ÷ visits), what's included (website only, returns not deducted), the period (calendar month) and the data source; differing definitions are a common reason two reports disagree.

A number alone means little: show each KPI against a comparison, such as the target, the previous month or the same month last year; for a seasonal business, prefer the same month last year, because December always beats November.

Leading indicators move before results do (visits, items added to baskets), while lagging indicators record results (revenue, returns); a balanced set shows both, so problems appear before they reach revenue.
Keep the set small, a handful per audience, and remember Goodhart's law, that a measure which becomes a target stops being a good measure: pushing conversion up by cutting prices can hurt profit.

lessons.title: Laying out a dashboard
objectives: Place the most important information where readers look first
Use KPI tiles with comparisons on a grid layout
Test a dashboard with the five-second test
key_points: Readers of left-to-right languages usually start at the top left, so put the most important KPIs there, in a row of tiles across the top, with trends below them and breakdowns and detail after that.
A KPI tile shows the label, the value in large type and its comparison, such as '▼ 94% of target', using an arrow or a sign as well as colour, so the direction never depends on colour alone.
Align everything to a grid, give related charts the same scales and colours, and group them with white space or a light box (enclosure) instead of heavy borders.
Fit the dashboard on one screen without scrolling where you can: every extra chart competes for attention, so remove any that don't support a decision.
The five-second test: show the dashboard to someone for five seconds and ask what they noticed; if they can't say how the business is doing, rework the layout or the tiles.

"""A one-page KPI dashboard for Lantern Lane's monthly review, December 2025."""
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

ch = pd.read_csv("monthly_channels.csv")
targets = pd.read_csv("targets_2025.csv")
BLUE, VERMILLION, GREY, DARK = "#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#BBBBBB", "#595959"


def kpis(year, month):
    """The month's KPIs, each defined in one place so every chart and tile agrees."""
    m = ch[(ch["year"] == year) & (ch["month"] == month)]
    web = m[m["channel"] == "website"]
    return {"Revenue": m["revenue"].sum(),
            "Orders": m["orders"].sum(),
            "Average order value": m["revenue"].sum() / m["orders"].sum(),
            "Website conversion": web["orders"].sum() / web["visits"].sum(),
            "Return rate": m["returns"].sum() / m["orders"].sum()}


now, last_month, last_year = kpis(2025, 12), kpis(2025, 11), kpis(2024, 12)
target = targets.loc[targets["month"] == 12, "revenue_target"].iloc[0]

hints: A change in a rate, from 2.71% to 2.46%, is -0.25 percentage points, or -9.3% in relative terms; say which you mean, and prefer points for rates.
December's revenue is far above November's every year, so the month-on-month change says more about the season than the business; the year-on-year change is the fairer comparison.
If the arrows (▲ ▼) show as boxes, your font lacks them: use + and - signs instead.

modules.title: Accessible, honest charts
modules.summary: Make charts and dashboards that everyone can read, recognise and fix the common ways charts mislead, and test your work with real readers before it's shared.

lessons.title: Designing for accessibility
objectives: Apply contrast, colour and text practices so charts work for more readers
Write alternative text and provide the data behind a chart
Make interactive dashboards usable with a keyboard and a screen reader
key_points: The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) ask for a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text and for the parts of a chart needed to understand it; a contrast checker gives the ratio for any two colours.
Never use colour as the only way to show meaning: add labels, patterns, line styles or symbols (▲ ▼), because colour vision deficiency is common and charts are often printed in greyscale.
Every chart shared digitally needs alternative text: what kind of chart it is, what it shows and its main finding; a complex chart also needs its data as a table, or a longer description nearby.

Interactive dashboards should work with a keyboard as well as a mouse, give filters and buttons clear text labels and keep a sensible reading order for screen readers; check the accessibility guidance of the tool you build with.
Plain language is accessibility too: short sentences, defined terms and numbers in context help readers with cognitive disabilities, readers working in a second language and busy readers alike.

walkthrough.title: Check chart colours against the WCAG ratios

steps.do: Open webaim.org/resources/contrastchecker in a browser.
Set Background Colour to #FFFFFF and Foreground Colour to #BBBBBB, the light grey used for context lines.

steps.see: 7:1, passing WCAG AA and AAA for normal text.

steps.see: Blue 5.19:1 passes for normal text; vermillion 3.87:1 passes for large text and graphical objects only; orange 2.25:1 fails even for graphical objects, so keep it for shading.

lessons.title: Misleading charts, and how to avoid them
objectives: Recognise the common ways charts mislead
Fix truncated axes, dual axes, cumulative charts and distorted areas
Check that comparisons are fair: the same periods, the same bases, rates instead of totals
key_points: A bar chart with a truncated axis exaggerates differences: with the axis starting at £400k, a 6.5% rise from £420k to £447k looks like a bar more than doubling; bars must start at zero.

Dual axes let the chart-maker pick two scales, so any two series can be made to look as if they move together or apart; show the ratio itself, index both series to 100 at a start date, or stack two charts one above the other.
A cumulative total can only rise while every value is positive, so it hides months that were worse than before; chart the monthly values, or the change on the same month last year, beside it.
Cherry-picked periods, uneven time intervals and missing context mislead without a single false number: show a full, regular period and the comparison that matters, such as the same months last year.
Areas, bubbles and pictograms must scale by area, not by width or radius, because doubling a circle's radius quadruples its area; 3-D effects distort sizes too, so avoid them for data.
Compare like with like: totals favour bigger groups, so use rates (per customer, per 1,000 visits) when groups differ in size, and say how many observations a percentage is based on.

lessons.title: Testing before you share
objectives: Check every number in a story or dashboard against its source
Test a chart or dashboard with someone from its audience
Document definitions, sources and refresh dates
key_points: Reconcile the numbers: totals should match the source system and each other, such as channel revenue adding up to total revenue; one wrong number costs trust in all the others.
Test with a real reader from the audience: ask them to explain the chart back in their own words, and where their explanation differs from your message, change the chart, not the reader.
Use a checklist before sharing: a title that states the finding, labelled axes and units, zero baselines for bars, accessible colours, alternative text, a source, a date and no unexplained jargon.
Document each dashboard: its purpose and audience, every KPI's definition, the data sources, when the data refreshes and who to contact, on the dashboard or one click away.
After release, watch how it's used and ask for feedback: remove what nobody looks at, and record changes to definitions so that this year's figures stay comparable with last year's.

w25 = web[web["year"] == 2025]
visits_change = w25["visits"].sum() / web.loc[web["year"] == 2024, "visits"].sum() - 1
orders_change = w25["orders"].sum() / web.loc[web["year"] == 2024, "orders"].sum() - 1
print(f"Website visits {visits_change:+.1%} but website orders {orders_change:+.1%} in 2025")
fig, (bad, good) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.5), layout="constrained")
bad.plot(w25["month"], w25["visits"], color=BLUE)
twin = bad.twinx()
twin.plot(w25["month"], w25["orders"], color=GREY)
bad.set_title("Misleading: two axes, two scales", loc="left", fontsize=10)
good.plot(w25["month"], w25["orders"] / w25["visits"] * 100, color=BLUE, marker="o")
good.set_ylim(0, 3.2)
good.set_title("Honest: show the ratio itself, conversion (%)", loc="left", fontsize=10)
fig.savefig("fix_2_dual_axis.png", dpi=120)
plt.close(fig)
steps.see: Website visits +4.4% but website orders -6.2% in 2025

steps.do: Build a cumulative revenue line next to a chart of the change on the same month of 2024.
steps.code:
# 3. A cumulative line always rises, so it hides the months when sales fell
monthly = web.pivot_table(index="month", columns="year", values="revenue", aggfunc="sum")
worse = int((monthly[2025] < monthly[2024]).sum())
print(f"Cumulative website revenue rose every month of 2025, yet it was below 2024 in {worse} of 12 months")
fig, (bad, good) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.5), layout="constrained")
bad.plot(monthly.index, monthly[2025].cumsum() / 1000, color=BLUE)
bad.set_title("Misleading alone: cumulative revenue (£k)", loc="left", fontsize=10)
diff = (monthly[2025] - monthly[2024]) / 1000
good.bar(diff.index, diff, color=[BLUE if d >= 0 else "#D55E00" for d in diff])
good.axhline(0, color=DARK, linewidth=0.8)
good.set_title("Honest: change on the same month of 2024 (£k)", loc="left", fontsize=10)
fig.savefig("fix_3_cumulative.png", dpi=120)
plt.close(fig)
print("Saved fix_1_baseline.png, fix_2_dual_axis.png and fix_3_cumulative.png")
steps.see: Cumulative website revenue rose every month of 2025, yet it was below 2024 in 7 of 12 months

hints: The distortion of a truncated bar is (value - axis start) ÷ (other value - axis start); with a zero start it's just the ratio of the values.
The bars in the third honest chart use colour and their position above or below the zero line, so the chart doesn't depend on colour alone.
Some charting tools start a column chart's axis above zero automatically when values are large and close: always check the axis minimum.

project.title: Tell the story of Lantern Lane's year, and build its dashboard
project.brief: Lantern Lane's two owners meet in January to review 2025 and plan 2026, and they've asked for three things. First, a one-page monthly KPI dashboard they can reuse every month: four to six KPIs, each precisely defined and compared with the target or the same month last year, laid out on a grid with the most important information first. Second, a story of five to seven charts, as slides or a document, structured as situation, complication and resolution, whose titles tell the story when read alone; it must cover the channel story and at least one finding from category_sales.csv (revenue by product category). Third, a one-page summary that leads with a recommendation and ends with the decision needed, its owner and a date, stating the assumptions behind any estimate. Use monthly_channels.csv, targets_2025.csv and category_sales.csv from the labs, and work in Python, a spreadsheet or both. Every chart must be accessible (contrast, never colour alone, alternative text) and honest (zero baselines for bars, no dual axes, fair comparisons). Before submitting, test the dashboard and the story with someone who hasn't seen the data, and act on what they say.
deliverables: The dashboard (an image, a PDF or a spreadsheet tab) and a table defining each KPI: formula, scope, period and source
The story: five to seven charts with action titles, in situation, complication and resolution order
A one-page summary: the big idea, the recommendation, supporting findings with their numbers, the decision, its owner and date, and the caveats
A pre-sharing checklist, completed, with what your test reader said and what you changed

rubric.name: Message and audience
rubric.description: One clear big idea for the owners, supported by correct numbers from the data, with a recommendation they can act on.

rubric.name: Narrative structure
rubric.description: Situation, complication and resolution in order, titles that tell the story when read alone, one point per chart, and detail kept to an appendix.

rubric.name: Chart design
rubric.description: The right chart for each comparison, clutter removed, colour used only for meaning, and annotation where the message depends on it.

rubric.name: Dashboard and KPIs
rubric.description: KPIs precisely defined and compared with a target or last year; the most important first, on a grid, on one screen.

rubric.name: Accessibility and honesty
rubric.description: Contrast checked, nothing shown by colour alone, alternative text for every chart, zero baselines for bars, no dual axes, caveats stated, and the test reader's feedback acted on.

project.submit: Paste or link your dashboard, your story (titles, charts and alternative text), your one-page summary, your KPI definitions and your completed checklist with the test reader's feedback.
